Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Musa was 19, African American, single, and working as a UX designer when he first spoke about the months that had altered the way he moved through ordinary life. The stalking began after he had briefly met a man through a social app and then ended the contact when the attention became unwanted. At first it was only messages that felt too frequent, then notes of where Musa had been, and then the unsettling certainty that this person was noticing him in the same places he went to every week. Musa remembered the escalation with particular clarity because it had turned familiar routines into scenes he now revisited in his mind with dread. Walking to his apartment door after work, he had once found signs that someone had been waiting nearby. On another day, he noticed the same car idling near his building and then again near the café where he liked to work on design drafts. He had come to believe that the world was dangerous in a way he had not understood before, that there were people who could watch, follow, and appear without warning in places that should have felt ordinary.

In the weeks after those incidents, Musa’s attention seemed to remain on alert even when nothing obvious was happening. He described moving through his day as if he had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next. That sense of constant watchfulness followed him into the smallest details of life: checking behind him before crossing the street, pausing when footsteps seemed to match his pace, scanning reflections in shop windows as he walked to his train. At work, where he spent long stretches designing interfaces on a laptop in a shared office, he found himself choosing seats with a clear view of the door and the glass wall, not because he expected trouble in any one moment, but because he could not settle unless he knew what was around him. Even then, his concentration was fragile. If a coworker mentioned an unexpected visitor in the lobby or if he noticed a phone buzzing repeatedly on the desk beside him, he would tense and look up quickly, as though he had to confirm immediately that nothing was about to happen.

Musa also described a heavy conviction that the event happened because of the way he acted. He replayed the early interactions and focused on his own choices with painful precision, wondering whether he had been too friendly, too direct, or too slow to recognize when the contact was becoming inappropriate. He was not saying that he had wanted what happened, but he kept returning to the thought that his own behavior must have opened the door to it. That belief made him scrutinize his past decisions and the way he interacted with others, especially men he met online. He had been careful, then doubting, then increasingly rigid about what he posted, who he replied to, and how much personal information he allowed into any conversation. He did not describe these changes as dramatic; rather, they had accumulated until he recognized that his social life had narrowed around caution.

Over time, the practical consequences became harder to ignore. Musa began taking different routes home from the office and timing his departures so he would not have to stand outside alone as long. He avoided lingering after work and often left group plans early, saying he was tired, though in truth he was watching the street, the parking lot, and the people who seemed to be walking too near his path. The café where he once enjoyed sketching wireframes became less usable because he could not relax when anyone entered and sat behind him. He found himself turning his chair to see the room or relocating to corners with walls behind him, and even then he remained unsettled. At home he double-checked locks and hesitated before opening the door, listening first for sounds in the hall. He knew these habits were making his life smaller, but the thought of being careless felt worse. What frightened him most was the possibility that he would miss the next sign, the next car, the next message, and that by the time he recognized danger it would already be too late.

By the time Musa sought help, he had reached a point where the tension had become difficult to hide. He was still functioning at work, but only by expending constant effort to stay on guard, and the strain was beginning to show in the way he avoided spontaneous plans and measured each outing against risk. He came to treatment not because the stalking had returned in exactly the same form, but because the fear had remained lodged in daily life long after the most obvious contact had stopped. He wanted to feel less trapped by the need to be careful, but he also admitted that he was afraid of trusting safety too soon.
